doc_title: NASA Mars 2020: MEDA Instrument Suite Overview
text: The Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA) is a suite of environmental sensors aboard NASA's Perseverance rover at Jezero Crater. MEDA measures ambient atmospheric pressure, air temperature at multiple heights (ATS), relative humidity, wind speed and direction, thermal infrared radiation from the surface, and atmospheric dust optical depth. MEDA's Air Temperature Sensors (ATS) consist of five sensors mounted around the rover mast and deck to minimize thermal contamination from the rover itself.

doc_title: NASA Mars 2020: MEDA Instrument Suite Overview
text: Ambient air temperature in Jezero Crater typically ranges from -85°C before sunrise to -15°C in the early afternoon during northern spring and summer. The MEDA Pressure Sensor (PS) employs a silicon piezoresistive transducer housed inside the rover warm electronics box with an external inlet port, achieving high precision measurements at 1 Hz resolution.

doc_title: Atmospheric Diurnal and Thermal Cycles in Jezero Crater
text: Meteorological observations in Jezero Crater (18.38°N, 77.58°E) demonstrate strong diurnal thermal swings driven by the low thermal inertia of the Martian surface and the extremely thin carbon dioxide atmosphere. Peak daytime temperatures occur between 13:00 and 15:00 Local True Solar Time (LTST), reaching typical values between -35°C and -10°C depending on season and dust loading. Minimum temperatures occur just prior to local dawn between 05:00 and 06:00 LTST, routinely dropping below -75°C.

doc_title: Atmospheric Diurnal and Thermal Cycles in Jezero Crater
text: Minimum temperatures occur just prior to local dawn between 05:00 and 06:00 LTST, routinely dropping below -75°C. Atmospheric pressure exhibits semi-diurnal solar thermal tides, with two daily maxima near 09:00 and 21:00 LTST, and two daily minima near 03:00 and 15:00 LTST. Seasonal changes in global surface pressure are controlled by the annual condensation and sublimation of carbon dioxide ice on the polar caps as solar longitude (Ls) progresses from 0° to 360°.

doc_title: Convective Vortices and Dust Devils in Jezero Crater
text: Intense surface heating around midday in Jezero Crater triggers violent dry convective boundary layer turbulence, generating numerous convective vortices and dust devils. When a convective vortex passes directly over or adjacent to the Perseverance rover, MEDA records an abrupt, sharp dip in atmospheric pressure, typically dropping by 20 to 60 Pascals over a span of tens of seconds to minutes.

doc_title: Convective Vortices and Dust Devils in Jezero Crater
text: Simultaneously, the temperature sensor often registers a transient thermal increase (+10°C to +30°C deviation above seasonal baseline) because the core of the vortex advects intensely superheated near-surface air upward. Dust optical sensors indicate sharp spikes in localized opacity during such vortex passages as dust grains are lifted and suspended into the boundary layer.

doc_title: Baroclinic Waves and Cold Front Passages on Mars
text: Traveling baroclinic synoptic weather systems and planetary waves frequently propagate through the northern mid-latitudes and subtropical fringes of Mars during northern autumn and winter. Cold front passages are marked by a rapid decrease in air temperature (-15°C to -25°C below the seasonal climatological mean) coupled with an increase in surface atmospheric pressure (+10 to +25 Pa). These fronts commonly arrive during pre-dawn or early morning hours, disrupting the calm nocturnal planetary boundary layer and generating gusty winds and low-level turbulence.

doc_title: Baroclinic Waves and Cold Front Passages on Mars
text: Such baroclinic systems can trigger localized or regional dust lifting events as they sweep across the Isidis Planitia basin into Jezero Crater.

doc_title: Atmospheric Gravity Waves and Mesoscale Pressure Surges
text: Mesoscale atmospheric gravity waves generated by airflow over the Jezero Crater rim and the Western Delta scarp induce oscillatory pressure perturbations on the crater floor. These pressure waves manifest as sudden positive or negative surges in atmospheric pressure (deviations exceeding 40 to 60 Pa above baseline) lasting from 2 to 6 hours. Because gravity waves are mechanical compressional disturbances, they often produce pronounced pressure anomalies with only modest or negligible shifts in local air temperature.

doc_title: Atmospheric Gravity Waves and Mesoscale Pressure Surges
text: Detecting an anomalous z-score in pressure exceeding 3.5σ without a corresponding large thermal spike is a classical signature of a passing atmospheric gravity wave train.

doc_title: Martian Dust Storm Dynamics and Atmospheric Heating
text: During regional and global Martian dust storms, massive quantities of micron-sized ferric oxide dust particles are lofted into the middle atmosphere (15–40 km altitude). Suspended dust absorbs incoming solar radiation, causing significant warming of the mid-troposphere while reducing sunlight reaching the surface, which attenuates the surface diurnal temperature range. At the surface, daytime maximum temperatures drop due to solar obscuration, while nighttime temperatures rise significantly because the elevated dust layer re-radiates thermal infrared downward like an insulating blanket.

doc_title: Martian Dust Storm Dynamics and Atmospheric Heating
text: Surface pressure drops persistently across large areas, accompanied by enhanced diurnal tidal harmonics and sustained atmospheric haze that can linger for dozens of Sols.

doc_title: Nocturnal Inversions and Radiative Nighttime Warming Events
text: Under clear Martian skies, radiative cooling normally produces an extremely strong nocturnal thermal inversion layer near the ground between 22:00 and 06:00 LTST. On specific nights, the advection of warm air aloft or the formation of high-altitude water-ice or dust clouds drastically increases downwelling longwave infrared flux. This produces anomalous nighttime warming, where the surface temperature can remain 20°C to 40°C warmer than expected for pre-dawn hours. Such events appear as positive thermal anomalies (>3σ) during the coldest hours of the Sol without corresponding pressure drops.

doc_title: Mars Orbit, Solar Longitude (Ls), and Seasonal Baselines
text:
The Martian year lasts 668.6 Martian days (Sols). Seasons are measured by Solar Longitude (Ls), defined as the angular position of Mars in its orbit around the Sun. Ls = 0° corresponds to the Northern Spring Equinox, Ls = 90° is Northern Summer Solstice (aphelion: Mars is farthest from Sun, cooler and cloudier),
Ls = 180° is Northern Autumn Equinox, and Ls = 270° is Northern Winter Solstice (perihelion: Mars is closest to Sun, warmer, windy, and dust-storm prone). Because Mars' orbit is noticeably eccentric (e ≈ 0.093), seasons in the northern hemisphere are of unequal length and intensity.

doc_title: Mars Orbit, Solar Longitude (Ls), and Seasonal Baselines
text: Statistical anomaly detection must always partition baselines by Ls season quadrant to avoid misclassifying natural orbital temperature shifts as anomalies.
